title: Critical AI Inference your CIO can Trust — Sahil Yadav, Hariharan Ganesan, Telemetrak
talk_summary: A vendor-style talk on 'trustworthy AI' (explainability, traceability, guardrails, human-in-the-loop) framed as 'XTOPS', with one real case study: a worker-safety IoT platform where GPS drift caused 70% false-positive alerts that users learned to ignore. The concrete mechanism worth copying is attribution telemetry that flags which input feature caused a bad inference, plus a human-notification/retrain loop.

takeaways.what_they_do: When an alert/inference is ignored or wrong, they trace back which input signal (GPS) drove it, so the root cause is identified automatically instead of by reading a complicated model.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there is no system to identify that GPS drift. We wouldn't know about it
takeaways.numbers: 70% false positives before fix; MTTR breakdown ~70% identifying problem, 20% finding solution

takeaways.what_they_do: They measured whether humans actually acted on AI alerts; when 70% were false positives, users stopped reacting, which was itself the failure mode.
takeaways.numbers: 70% false positives led to alert abandonment

takeaways.technique: Guardrail that pauses and escalates to human
takeaways.what_they_do: Adaptive control: if the system drifts or makes a wrong decision, it slows down, changes course, or calls a human with the right context.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the system should be able to slow down, change its course, or at least call a human for help

takeaways.technique: MTTR for explainable errors as an ops metric
takeaways.what_they_do: They define MTRE (mean time to resolve explainable errors) as the time from an unexpected failure to understanding the 'why' and shipping a fix.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the time that takes for us to fix something unexpected when it happens to how quickly can we understand the why
takeaways.numbers: Case study: 8 months to solve first time, then ~7 days once framework existed
